newsitem.title: UK: Fare curbs would stay if Tube sold - UK govt source.
newsitem.headline: Fare curbs would stay if Tube sold - UK govt source.

text.p: Any privatisation of London's underground rail network, London Underground, or the Tube, would likely protect consumers with fare controls and via regulations requiring minimum service standards, a government source said.

"The key selling point of (national) rail privatisation to consumers was provision of fare controls and the need to maintain existing levels of service," the source told Reuters on Wednesday. "So it is unlikely that those would not be maintained under the London Underground sale."
He called recent press reports suggesting otherwise "not true."

Despite the great controversy around the nearly-complete process of rail privatisation over the last three years, the Conservative government is currently evaluating its options on how it could privatise the Underground network.
The impending general election, which must be held by May 22, has heightened the political profile of the issue in London where the future of public transport is seen as a key concern.
A report in the Wednesday's Financial Times suggested that the government may have to pay future private sector owners to take the network off its hands.
The Department of Transport refused to comment on this.
Officials also said they had no comment on whether a sale may be announced this week, as some papers said at the weekend.
However, the government source said any decision to sell would be underpinned by factors that included the financial aspects, practicality and the impact on voter sentiment.
The options under consideration are understood to include a single sell-off and selling off the metro's lines separately.

This latter type of piecemeal line sale would be possible because London Underground already runs each of its lines as a separate business with its own fleet of rolling stock. It would parallel the method for privatising national passenger trains.
Some newspapers have suggested that Railtrack, the recently privatised national rail infrastructure group, would be interested in taking over London's underground infrastructure.
Transport insiders say the issue had now become a political football as the election approaches.
The government source said, "In a pre-election situation the government has to have reasons to do it which are presentable in the public eye."
